tip: Some verbs shift 'e' to 'i' in the 'er' form: 'vergessen' becomes 'er vergisst', while the infinitive keeps the 'e'.
Passive is a form of 'werden' plus a past participle. Past passive uses 'wurde': 'das Problem wurde endlich gelöst' = it was finally solved.
The verb 'werden' plus an infinitive builds the future: 'wir werden uns nächste Woche treffen' = we will meet next week. The infinitive 'treffen' goes to the end.
German often uses the present for the future when a time word is given: 'wir sehen uns nächste Woche' means we will see each other next week.
With two objects the person is usually dative and the thing accusative: 'seinem Chef' comes before 'eine Nachricht'.
The verb 'aufhören' is separable, so in a command the prefix splits off and follows the verb: 'hör auf' = stop.
For days and weekends German uses 'am', short for 'an dem': 'am Wochenende' = on the weekend, 'am Montag' = on Monday.
The fixed phrase 'es zieht' means there is a draft. The 'es' is a dummy subject with no real thing behind it.
The 'ihr' command is just the 'ihr' verb form without the pronoun: 'ihr esst' becomes 'esst', 'ihr genießt' becomes 'genießt'.
With movement across, 'über' takes the accusative: 'über den gefrorenen Teich' shows motion, so 'den', not 'dem'.
The polite command puts the verb first, then 'Sie': 'lesen Sie bitte'. The pronoun 'Sie' stays, unlike in the 'du' or 'ihr' command.
The word 'bevor' sends its verb to the very end of the clause: 'bevor ich hinausgehe', not 'bevor ich gehe hinaus'.
The word 'außerhalb' takes the genitive: 'außerhalb der Geschäftszeiten' = outside business hours. That is why it is 'der', not 'die'.
Comparatives normally add '-er' and use 'als' for than: 'teuer' becomes 'teurer', dropping the second 'e', so 'teurer als' = more expensive than.
When a time phrase opens the sentence, the verb stays second and the subject follows: 'Gestern Abend beobachtete der Astronom'.
Verbs of motion usually form the perfect with 'sein', not 'haben': 'wir sind ... gereist' = we traveled. The participle 'gereist' goes last.
A modal like 'können' pushes the main verb to the end as an infinitive: 'wir können nicht anfangen' = we cannot start.
The verb 'sich treffen mit' needs the reflexive 'dich': 'du dich mit Freunden triffst' = you meet up with friends. Drop 'dich' and 'treffen' means to hit or run into.
The word 'wegen' takes the genitive: 'wegen des Streiks' = because of the strike. That genitive is why it reads 'des Streiks', not 'der Streik'.
The verb 'sein' has an irregular 'ihr' command: 'seid pünktlich' = be on time, said to several people. It is 'seid', not 'seit'.
The word 'deren' means 'whose', the possessive relative word: 'die Lehrerin, deren Unterricht...' = the teacher whose lessons...
'Patient' is an n-noun: outside the nominative it adds '-en', so 'dem Patienten', not 'dem Patient'.
Passive under a modal is a participle plus 'werden': 'muss dringend repariert werden' = must urgently be repaired, with 'werden' in its base form.
The pattern 'um' plus 'zu' plus a verb expresses purpose: 'um besser Deutsch zu lernen' = in order to learn German better.
In a 'dass'-clause the conjugated verb moves to the very end: 'dass du kommen konntest' closes with 'konntest'.
German builds the passive with 'werden' plus a past participle, and that participle goes last: 'wird sofort bezahlt'.
For a passive in the past, use 'wurde', the past of 'werden': 'das Paket wurde heute geliefert'.
The verb 'sein' has an irregular 'Sie'-command: it is 'seien Sie', never 'sind Sie'.
Motion verbs like 'fahren' usually form the perfect with 'sein', not 'haben': 'er gefahren ist'.
With separable verbs, 'zu' slots inside the word: 'ausschalten' becomes 'auszuschalten'.
